derivations.claim: Uniqueness in [F2] gives linearity of $A^*$: for scalars $a,b$ and $y_1,y_2\in Y$, conjugate-linearity of the second slot shows that $aA^*y_1+bA^*y_2$ satisfies the defining identity for $ay_1+by_2$, so it equals $A^*(ay_1+by_2)$. For $w=A^*y$, [F2], [F4] and [F7] give $\|w\|^2=\langle Aw,y\rangle\le|\langle Aw,y\rangle|\le\|A\|\|w\|\|y\|$. Dividing when $w\ne0$, and treating $w=0$ directly, proves $\|A^*y\|\le\|A\|\|y\|$. Thus $A^*$ is bounded, and composition and addition make $B_\lambda$ linear and bounded with $\|B_\lambda x\|\le(\|A\|^2+\lambda)\|x\|$. The adjoint identity and conjugate symmetry [F6] give $\langle B_\lambda x,z\rangle=\langle Ax,Az\rangle+\lambda\langle x,z\rangle=\langle x,B_\lambda z\rangle$ for all $x,z\in X$. In particular, $\langle B_\lambda x,x\rangle=\|Ax\|^2+\lambda\|x\|^2\ge\lambda\|x\|^2$.

By [F4], $\|B_\lambda x\|\,\|x\|\ge |\langle B_\lambda x,x\rangle|=\langle B_\lambda x,x\rangle\ge \lambda\|x\|^2$. Thus $\|B_\lambda x\|\ge\lambda\|x\|$ for $x\ne0$; the same inequality is trivial for $x=0$. Hence $B_\lambda$ is injective. If $B_\lambda x_n$ converges, this inequality applied to $x_n-x_m$ makes $(x_n)$ Cauchy; completeness of $X$ and boundedness of $B_\lambda$ show its limit lies in $\operatorname{ran}B_\lambda$. Therefore the range is closed.

If $z\in(\operatorname{ran}B_\lambda)^\perp$, [F8] gives $\langle z,B_\lambda x\rangle=0$ for every $x\in X$. By conjugate symmetry [F6] this is $\langle B_\lambda x,z\rangle=0$, and the symmetry identity from step 1.1 gives $\langle x,B_\lambda z\rangle=0$ for every $x\in X$. Taking $x=B_\lambda z$ and using positive definiteness [F6] yields $B_\lambda z=0$; injectivity from step 2.1 then gives $z=0$. Thus the closed range has zero orthogonal complement.

By [F5] and the Countable Choice assumption [A1], a closed subspace with zero orthogonal complement is all of $X$; so $B_\lambda$ is surjective as well as injective. For $y=B_\lambda x$, step 2.1 gives $\|B_\lambda^{-1}y\|=\|x\|\le\|y\|/\lambda$, proving $\|B_\lambda^{-1}\|\le1/\lambda$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $X$ and $Y$ be real or complex
Hilbert spaces and let $A:X\to Y$ be bounded, with Hilbert adjoint $A^*$. For
$\lambda>0$, define

$$B_\lambda:=A^*A+\lambda I_X.$$

Then $B_\lambda:X\to X$ is bijective and

$$\|B_\lambda^{-1}\|\le\frac1\lambda.$$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let
$A:X\to Y$ be bounded, with Hilbert adjoint $A^*$. For $\lambda>0$, put
$R_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*$, which is well-defined by
[[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]]. Then for every $g\in Y$,

$$\|R_\lambda g\|\le\frac{\|g\|}{2\sqrt\lambda},\qquad \|R_\lambda\|\le\frac1{2\sqrt\lambda}.$$

The proof uses the normal equation and the Hilbert-space inner product; it
does not use a compact-operator convergence rate or a source condition.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ and $K$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,K)$ be a bounded linear operator ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]], [[def-space-of-bounded-linear-operators]]). For fixed $y\in K$ the map

$$x\longmapsto\langle Tx,y\rangle_K$$

is a bounded linear functional on $H$: it is linear in $x$ because $T$ is linear and the pairing is linear in its first argument, and $|\langle Tx,y\rangle_K|\le\|Tx\|\,\|y\|\le\|T\|\,\|x\|\,\|y\|$ by Cauchy–Schwarz and the operator-norm inequality ([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]], [[def-operator-norm]]). By Riesz representation ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]) there is therefore a unique vector $T^*y\in H$ with

$$\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H\qquad\text{for every }x\in H .$$

The **Hilbert adjoint** of $T$ is the map

$$T^*:K\longrightarrow H,\qquad y\longmapsto T^*y .$$

It is the unique map $K\to H$ satisfying the displayed identity, since two such maps have $\langle x,(T^*_1-T^*_2)y\rangle=0$ for all $x$ and hence $(T^*_1-T^*_2)y=0$ by positive definiteness.

**The dictionary with the Banach transpose.** Write $R_H:H\to H^*$ and $R_K:K\to K^*$ for the Riesz maps $R_H(x)=\langle\,\cdot\,,x\rangle_H$ and $R_K(y)=\langle\,\cdot\,,y\rangle_K$, and let $T'\in\mathcal B(K^*,H^*)$ be the transpose of $T$, $(T'g)(x)=g(Tx)$ ([[def-transpose-of-a-bounded-operator]]). Then for all $y\in K$ and $x\in H$,

$$\bigl(R_H(T^*y)\bigr)(x)=\langle x,T^*y\rangle_H=\langle Tx,y\rangle_K=(R_Ky)(Tx)=\bigl(T'(R_Ky)\bigr)(x),$$

so $R_H\,T^*=T'\,R_K$. The Hilbert adjoint is thus the Banach transpose conjugated by the Riesz identifications of $H$ and $K$ with their duals; it is a different operator from $T'$ whenever the Riesz maps are conjugate-linear.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, let $b\in\mathbb F^m$, and let
$\lambda\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\lambda>0$. The **Tikhonov regularised
least-squares objective** is the map

$$ J_\lambda(x):=\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2 \qquad(x\in\mathbb F^n), $$

where $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the Euclidean norm induced by the standard inner product
([[def-inner-product-norm]]).

The parameter $\lambda$ is part of the problem data. The second term penalises
large norms of $x$, so the regularised problem is not the same optimisation
problem as the unregularised least-squares problem.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, let $b\in\mathbb F^m$, and let
$\lambda\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\lambda>0$. Then
the Tikhonov objective

$$J_\lambda(x)=\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2$$

is strictly convex and has the unique minimiser

$$x_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*b.$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A linear map $T:X\to Y$
([[def-linear-map]]) is a **compact operator** when the image of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]); explicitly, for every bounded $A\subseteq X$ the
closure $\overline{T(A)}$ in $Y$ is a compact subset of $Y$. The set of compact
operators $X\to Y$ is written $\mathcal K(X,Y)$. The metric used here is $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$, supplied over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]].

**The closed unit ball suffices.** Put
$\overline B_X:=\{x\in X:\|x\|\le 1\}$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Then $T$ is compact if and only if
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$.

Indeed, if $T$ is compact then $\overline B_X$ is bounded, because
$\overline B_X\subseteq B(0,2)$ while $B(0,2)$ is bounded and a subset of a
bounded set is bounded, so $T(\overline B_X)$ has compact closure. Conversely
assume $\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ compact and let $A\subseteq X$ be bounded.
If $A=\varnothing$ then $T(A)=\varnothing$, whose closure is empty and hence
compact. Otherwise $A\subseteq B(x_0,r)$ for some $x_0\in X$ and real $r>0$, so
every $x\in A$ satisfies $\|x\|\le\|x_0\|+r=:R$; if $R>0$ then
$A\subseteq R\,\overline B_X$ and if $R=0$ then $A\subseteq\{0\}$, so in either
case $T(A)\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$. Scalar multiplication by
$R$ is continuous ([[lem-vector-operations-are-continuous-in-a-normed-space]]),
so $R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a compact subset of $Y$
([[thm-compactness-under-continuous-maps]]), hence closed
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]); therefore
$\overline{T(A)}\subseteq R\,\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is a closed subset of a
compact set, hence compact, and $T$ is compact.

**A compact operator is bounded.** If $T$ is compact then the compact set
$\overline{T(\overline B_X)}$ is bounded
([[thm-compact-subset-is-closed-and-bounded]]), so there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|Tx\|\le C$ for every $x\in\overline B_X$ and hence $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$ for
every $x\in X$; thus $T$ is a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). This is a consequence of compactness, not a
hypothesis of the definition.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $V$ be a real or complex inner-product space with induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. Then $\|v\|\ge0$ with $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, $\|\lambda v\|=|\lambda|\,\|v\|$ for every scalar $\lambda$, and $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$; hence $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm on $V$, read over $\mathbb R$ by [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and over $\mathbb C$ by [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]].

Let stored $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$ and $y\in\mathbb F^m$ be real or complex, $m,n\ge1$, and let stored real $\lambda>0$. Let $x_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*y$. Compute $\alpha=\operatorname{fl}(\sqrt\lambda)>0$ under the successful normal-range square-root model, and solve the stored augmented problem $\min_x\|[A;\alpha I]x-[y;0]\|_2$ by scaled Householder QR and rounded substitution. For complex inputs use the realification described below, so the backend uses only real triangular divisions. Every operation must succeed; failed pivots, invalid operations and out-of-range nonzero intermediates return range-failure.

For any returned $\widehat x$, evaluate $\widehat r$ and its certified allowance $\rho$ by [[lem-rounded-linear-and-normal-residual-certificates]] for the intended residual $r=(A^*A+\lambda I)\widehat x-A^*y$. Then
$$\|\widehat x-x_\lambda\|_2\le\frac{\|\widehat r\|_2+\rho}{\lambda}.$$
This bounds returned-output roundoff relative to the exact direct-solve target $x_{\rm stop}=x_\lambda$. It also certifies the solve term in any larger analytic error chain, irrespective of the backend. The representation of $\sqrt\lambda$ contributes no hidden change of target: $|\alpha^2-\lambda|\le(2u+u^2)\lambda$. If residual evaluation instead uses exact $\alpha^2$, add $|\alpha^2-\lambda|\|\widehat x\|_2$ to its allowance; rounding a computed $\alpha^2$ needs its own scalar error as well.

The backend's nearby least-squares conclusion holds under the completed QR/solve hypotheses and nonsingularity condition. In real dimension, write $C=[A;\alpha I]$ and $\epsilon_Q=\beta_Q\|C\|_F$. A sufficient check is $\epsilon_Q<\alpha$ and $\|\Delta R\|_F<\alpha-\epsilon_Q$. An explicit certified nonsingularity check may replace this sufficient margin.

For a Hilbert-space discrete operator, supply isometries $U:\mathbb F^n\to X$ and $V:\mathbb F^m\to Y$ with $A_h=VAU^*$, and return $U\widehat x$. With coefficient datum $y_c=V^*y_\delta$, the exact normal solution lies in $\operatorname{ran}U$ and the coefficient residual lifts isometrically, so the same certificate applies to $r_h$; likewise use $V^*y_{h,\delta}$ for $r_{h,h}$. If a stored coefficient datum $\widehat y_c$ differs from $V^*y$ by at most $\epsilon_y$, add $\|A\|_2\epsilon_y$ to the residual allowance. If the returned output also has an orthogonal component $z\perp\operatorname{ran}U$ of norm at most $\epsilon_\perp$, add $\lambda\epsilon_\perp$. Finite rank alone does not supply these coordinate or output certificates.

derivations.claim: By [F7], $A$ is bounded, and [F8] supplies the Hilbert-space hypotheses. By [F1], both shifted normal operators are invertible, so the displayed $R_\lambda$ and $R_{\lambda,h}$ are defined. Multiplying their definitions by their normal operators gives $(A^*A+\lambda I)R_\lambda=A^*$ and $(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I)R_{\lambda,h}=A_h^*$.

Adding and subtracting the intermediate vectors $R_\lambda y$, $R_\lambda y_\delta$, and $R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta$ cancels the intervening terms and proves the stated four-term identity. Since $y_\delta=y+e$, [F2] gives $\|R_\lambda y-R_\lambda y_\delta\|=\|R_\lambda e\| \le\delta/(2\sqrt\lambda)$.

Adding and subtracting $x_{\mathrm{stop}}$ gives the optional stopping/roundoff identity. The normal equation for $R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta$ and the definition of $r_{\mathrm{stop}}$ imply $(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I)(x_{\mathrm{stop}}-R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta) =r_{\mathrm{stop}}$. By [F1], the stopping term is at most $\|r_{\mathrm{stop}}\|/\lambda$; the other term is exactly the stated roundoff difference.

In the refined datum case, $y_\delta-y_{h,\delta}=(Ax^\dagger+e)-(A_hx^\dagger+e)=d_h$. Inserting $R_\lambda y_{h,\delta}$ and $R_{\lambda,h}y_{h,\delta}$ into the chain therefore gives the displayed five-term identity by cancellation.

Let $z=R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta$. The normal equation in step 1.1 gives $(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I)(\widetilde x-z)=r_h$. By [F1], $\|\widetilde x-z\|\le\|r_h\|/\lambda$. The triangle inequality [F9] applied to the four-term identity, using step 1.2 for its noise term, proves the stated total error bound.

Applying [F2] to $d_h$ bounds its pre-inversion contribution by $\|R_\lambda d_h\|\le\|d_h\|/(2\sqrt\lambda)$. Applying [F1] to $r_{h,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I)(\widetilde x_h-R_{\lambda,h}y_{h,\delta})$ gives the stated refined solve-residual bound. Under the residual-evaluation hypothesis, the triangle inequality [F9] gives $\|r_{h,h}\|\le\|\widehat r_{h,h}\|+\rho_{h,h}$.

By [F4], an assumed operator-norm bound $\|R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h}\|\le\eta_{\lambda,h}$ gives $\|(R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h})y_\delta\| \le\eta_{\lambda,h}\|y_\delta\|$. Also, the triangle inequality [F9] gives $\|r_h\|\le\|\widehat r_h\|+\|r_h-\widehat r_h\| \le\|\widehat r_h\|+\rho_h$ under the stated residual-evaluation hypothesis. These are conditional estimates, not automatic stability claims.

In the finite-matrix case with $A_h=A$ and the exact regularized output $\widetilde x=R_\lambda y_\delta$, [F5]–[F6] identify $R_\lambda$ with the canonical Tikhonov minimizer. The baseline identity from step 1.2 then reduces to the displayed finite-matrix bias/noise formula.

For stored finite data, or for supplied isometric coordinates $A_h=VMU^*$ and returned output $U\widehat x$, apply [F10] to the coefficient matrix $M$ (the matrix case uses identity embeddings) and datum $g=y_\delta$ or $g=y_{h,\delta}$. The exact normal residual lifts isometrically to $r_h$ or $r_{h,h}$, with any certified coordinate-data and orthogonal-output allowances from [F10]. Hence steps 2.2 and 3.1 apply. For the exact direct augmented solve, $x_{\mathrm{stop}}=R_{\lambda,h}g$, and [F10] bounds the returned-output term by $(\|\widehat r\|+\rho)/\lambda$. The analytic identity and its independent bias, noise and discretization terms are unchanged.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Let $X,Y$ be real or complex Hilbert spaces, let
$A:X\to Y$ be compact (hence bounded), and let $A_h:X\to Y$ be a bounded
discrete operator whose range is a finite-dimensional subspace of $Y$. For
$\lambda>0$,
define

$$R_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A^*,\qquad R_{\lambda,h}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)^{-1}A_h^*.$$

These maps are well-defined by [[lem-hilbert-tikhonov-normal-operator-invertible]]. Let $x^\dagger\in X$, $y=Ax^\dagger$, $y_\delta=y+e$ with $\|e\|\le\delta$ and $\delta\ge0$, and let $\widetilde x\in X$. Define the exact discrete normal-equation residual

$$r_h=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)\widetilde x-A_h^*y_\delta.$$

Then the following chain is exact:

$$x^\dagger-\widetilde x=(x^\dagger-R_\lambda y) +(R_\lambda y-R_\lambda y_\delta) +(R_\lambda y_\delta-R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta) +(R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta-\widetilde x).$$

Its norm satisfies

$$\|x^\dagger-\widetilde x\|\le \|x^\dagger-R_\lambda y\|+\frac{\delta}{2\sqrt\lambda} +\|(R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h})y_\delta\|+\frac{\|r_h\|}{\lambda}.$$

The first term is regularization bias, the second is data noise, the third is the regularized-operator discretization difference, and the fourth is the solve residual. The third term receives a numerical bound only when an operator-perturbation bound is supplied: if $\|R_\lambda-R_{\lambda,h}\|\le\eta_{\lambda,h}$, it is at most $\eta_{\lambda,h}\|y_\delta\|$. If residual evaluation returns $\widehat r_h$ with a certified $\|r_h-\widehat r_h\|\le\rho_h$, the last term is at most $(\|\widehat r_h\|+\rho_h)/\lambda$. If an algorithm has a specified exact-arithmetic stopping output $x_{\mathrm{stop}}$ and returns a computed output $\widetilde x$, the last difference can further split as

$$R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta-\widetilde x= (R_{\lambda,h}y_\delta-x_{\mathrm{stop}}) +(x_{\mathrm{stop}}-\widetilde x).$$

Writing $r_{\mathrm{stop}}=(A_h^*A_h+\lambda I_X)x_{\mathrm{stop}} -A_h^*y_\delta$, the first term is at most $\|r_{\mathrm{stop}}\|/\lambda$; the second is the separate returned-output roundoff term. Any bound on that roundoff or on residual-evaluation error requires its own arithmetic hypotheses. Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $x\in\mathbb F^n$, $y\in\mathbb F^m$ have stored real or complex entries, with $m,n\ge1$. Use the operationwise arithmetic model, successful sequential dot products, and $0<u<1$ with $(\max(m,n)-1)u<1$. Define
$$g_k=\frac{1+6u}{1-(k-1)u}-1,\qquad F=\|A\|_F,\quad X=\|x\|_2,\quad Y=\|y\|_2.$$
For $\widehat v=\operatorname{fl}(Ax)$ and $\widehat w=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat v-y)$, put $V=g_nFX$ and $W=V+u(\|\widehat v\|_2+Y)$. Then
$$\|\widehat w-(Ax-y)\|_2\le W.$$
For a stored real $\lambda>0$, also compute $\widehat z=\operatorname{fl}(A^*\widehat w)$, $\widehat l=\operatorname{fl}(\lambda x)$ and $\widehat r=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat z+\widehat l)$, rounding scalar multiplication componentwise. The exact intended normal residual $r=A^*(Ax-y)+\lambda x$ satisfies
$$\|\widehat r-r\|_2\le\rho:=FW+g_mF\|\widehat w\|_2+u\lambda X+u(\|\widehat z\|_2+\|\widehat l\|_2).$$
Norms in these certificates mean exact norms or certified upper bounds. Uncontrolled rounding of the certificate itself is not authorized. The linear bound applies columnwise to certify $\|I-AB\|_2\le\|I-AB\|_F$ from stored basis-solve columns $B$.

Let $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$, $m\ge n\ge1$, have full column rank. Successful scaled Householder QR gives the exactly orthonormal reduced representative $\widehat Q$ and computed triangular $\widehat R$ with
$$A+\Delta_Q=\widehat Q\widehat R,\qquad \|\Delta_Q\|_F\le\beta_Q\|A\|_F,\qquad \beta_Q=(1+\kappa_m)^n-1,$$
where $\kappa_m$ is the proved local-step coefficient. Apply the stored reflectors to $b$ by rounded rank-one updates and let $\widehat y$ be the first $n$ coordinates. Set $\beta_b=\beta_Q$. Alternatively, if an explicitly supplied exactly orthonormal $\widehat Q$ has entries admissible as arithmetic inputs and $\widehat y=\operatorname{fl}(\widehat Q^Tb)$ uses sequential rounded dots, set $\beta_b=\sqrt n\,\gamma_m$. Solve $\widehat R\widehat x=\widehat y$ by successful rounded back substitution. Suppose $mu<1$ and $\gamma_{n+3}<1/8$. There exist $\delta b$ and upper triangular $\Delta R$ with
$$(\widehat R+\Delta R)\widehat x=\widehat Q^T(b+\delta b),\qquad \|\delta b\|_2\le\beta_b\|b\|_2,\qquad \|\Delta R\|_F\le\gamma_{n+3}\|\widehat R\|_F.$$
If $\widehat R+\Delta R$ is nonsingular, $\widehat x$ is the unique least-squares solution for $\widetilde A=\widehat Q(\widehat R+\Delta R)$ and $\widetilde b=b+\delta b$. The relative matrix perturbation is at most $\beta_Q+\gamma_{n+3}(1+\beta_Q)$; the right-hand perturbation is at most $\beta_b$. Consequently the formerly stated weaker factor $20\gamma_{n+3}$ bound also holds. Success and nonsingularity are explicit hypotheses.

Let the representable set, normal range, and unit roundoff be as in [[def-standard-relative-floating-point-model-and-unit-roundoff]]. Here fl is round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, on each real exact result that is zero or normal; every other nonzero exact result (subnormal or overflow), NaN, infinity, invalid operation, or division by zero returns range-failure. A real add, subtract, multiply, or divide is one rounded operation. For positive in-range x, fl(sqrt(x)) is correctly rounded to nearest, ties-to-even, and fails unless its result is positive and normal. A real fused multiply-add returns the correctly rounded value of the single exact expression ab+c; it is not two operations.

Complex addition and subtraction round real and imaginary components separately. A complex product (a+ib)(c+id) uses four rounded real products ac, bd, ad, bc, then rounded subtraction and addition, for six real operations. Conjugation and sign changes are exact. Scaling and division by a positive real scalar round each complex component separately; no other complex division primitive is used here.

A procedure succeeds only when each exact intermediate is zero or normal and every rounded output is finite; otherwise it returns the first range-failure with its operation or pivot index. For ku<1 write gamma_k=ku/(1-ku). This is a no-underflow success model, not the gradual-underflow model.

Let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, let $b\in\mathbb F^m$, and let
$\lambda\in\mathbb R$ satisfy $\lambda>0$. Then
the Tikhonov objective

$$J_\lambda(x)=\|Ax-b\|_2^2+\lambda\|x\|_2^2$$

is strictly convex and has the unique minimiser

$$x_\lambda=(A^*A+\lambda I)^{-1}A^*b.$$

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Under the sufficient margin, the further triangular perturbation preserves a positive lower bound. Thus the nonsingularity premise in [F2] holds under the stated check. The theorem still explicitly requires successful arithmetic; exact full rank alone does not ensure rounded success.

By [F3], $\alpha=\sqrt\lambda(1+\delta)$, $|\delta|\le u$, whence $|\alpha^2-\lambda|\le(2u+u^2)\lambda$. For any $z$, Cauchy-Schwarz gives $\|(A^*A+\lambda I)z\|\|z\|\ge\langle(A^*A+\lambda I)z,z\rangle=\|Az\|^2+\lambda\|z\|^2\ge\lambda\|z\|^2$. The normal equation [F4] therefore implies $\|\widehat x-x_\lambda\|\le\|r\|/\lambda\le(\|\widehat r\|+\rho)/\lambda$ by [F1]. Replacing the coefficient in a residual by $\alpha^2$ changes that exact residual by $(\alpha^2-\lambda)\widehat x$, giving the stated additional allowance.

For complex inputs identify $z=z_R+iz_I$ with $(z_R,z_I)\in\mathbb R^{2n}$. The real matrix $A_R=\begin{pmatrix}\operatorname{Re}A&-\operatorname{Im}A\\\operatorname{Im}A&\operatorname{Re}A\end{pmatrix}$ represents exactly the same linear map, preserves vector norms, and satisfies $\|A_R\|_2=\|A\|_2$, $\|A_R\|_F=\sqrt2\|A\|_F$ by direct component sums. Apply [F2] to $[A_R;\alpha I_{2n}]$ and datum $((\operatorname{Re}y,\operatorname{Im}y),0)$; this is exactly the original complex objective. In the supplied Hilbert representation, $U^*U=I$, $V^*V=I$, and $A_h^*=UA^*V^*$. For every coefficient vector $e$, put $w=A^*e$. Then $\|w\|_2^2=\langle Aw,e\rangle\le|\langle Aw,e\rangle|\le\|A\|_2\|w\|_2\|e\|_2$ by [F5]–[F6]; dividing for $w\ne0$ (and checking $w=0$ directly) gives $\|A^*e\|_2\le\|A\|_2\|e\|_2$.
